analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil company windfall profits and uses the money to help consumers pay energy bills.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors, never getting a hearing, a vote, or action in any of the four committees it was sent to before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced during the 2008 gas price spike, this bill would have stripped major integrated oil companies of a domestic production tax deduction, imposed a 25% windfall profits tax on profits above their inflation-adjusted 2002-2006 average, and put that money into a fund for low-income heating assistance, home weatherization, and help buying efficient cars and appliances. It also would have made price gouging during declared energy emergencies illegal, let the government sue OPEC in US courts, and required regulators to raise margin requirements and police offshore oil trading to curb speculation.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing high gasoline and heating bills, especially low-income families who would get expanded heating assistance (LIHEAP) and weatherization; consumers who would gain federal and state enforcement against price gouging during emergencies; and buyers of hybrid and energy-efficient vehicles and appliances, who would get purchase assistance.

how_it_helps.text: Channels revenues from new oil company taxes into expanded Low Income Home Energy Assistance, home weatherization, and help buying efficient cars and appliances.

Makes it unlawful to charge 'unconscionably excessive' prices for gasoline and other fuels during a presidentially declared energy emergency, enforceable by the FTC and state attorneys general, with penalties up to three times the profit.
Extends Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority to energy derivatives and requires higher margin levels and foreign-exchange transparency to curb excessive oil speculation.
Removes foreign oil states' sovereign immunity so the US Attorney General can sue cartels like OPEC for restricting production or fixing oil prices.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies, which would lose a domestic production tax deduction and pay a 25% excise tax on profits above their 2002-2006 average; oil futures traders, who would face higher margin costs; and foreign oil-producing states, which could face US antitrust suits. Some of the oil tax burden could ultimately be passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big oil companies and oil traders

drawbacks.text: Windfall profits taxes can reduce oil companies' incentive and capital to invest in production and refining, and some of the added tax cost could be passed on to consumers in fuel prices.

The price gouging ban only applies during presidentially declared emergencies, and its 'unconscionably excessive' standard could be hard to enforce where prices reflect genuine market-wide conditions, which the definition explicitly excludes from liability.
Lawsuits against OPEC under the NOPEC provision could provoke retaliation against US oil companies and diplomatic friction with producer nations.
Higher margin requirements on oil futures could reduce market liquidity, and critics disputed how much speculation actually drove 2008 oil prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer benefits — heating assistance, anti-gouging enforcement, and speculation curbs — would come at a real cost to the largest oil companies, and a well-run economy argument exists that taxing windfall profits or suing OPEC raises prices or risks retaliation. The design was detailed and enforcement mechanisms were concrete, but the burden of the oil taxes could partially reach consumers. As a single-sponsor bill it was never tested in committee, so its workability was never examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and three subcommittees the day it was introduced, and none of them ever held a markup or vote on it, so it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 30, 2008, when crude oil traded near $120 a barrel and gasoline cost more than $3.50 a gallon, roughly double 2001 levels.

The same day, the House referred it to four committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, and Judiciary — splitting its tax, consumer protection, antitrust, and commodities provisions across different panels.
It was referred to three subcommittees, including Energy and Air Quality and Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, but none of the committees or subcommittees ever reported it or held a vote.
No other House member cosponsored the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major integrated oil companies kept their domestic production tax deduction and faced no windfall profits tax, oil futures traders avoided new margin and disclosure requirements, and OPEC remained shielded from US antitrust suits. No consumer received the bill's proposed heating assistance or gouging protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies and oil traders

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the sponsor attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split on this version was never tested, though its oil tax provisions resembled Democratic proposals of the era.

industries.note: The bill denies them the Section 199 domestic production deduction, taxes foreign oil and gas income more strictly, and imposes a 25% excise tax on profits above their inflation-adjusted 2002-2006 average. Their record 2008 profits were the direct funding source for the bill's consumer aid.

industries.industry: Oil and energy commodity traders and speculators
industries.note: The bill extends CFTC authority to energy derivatives, requires margin increases on crude oil trades, and forces foreign exchanges trading US-delivered oil to publish position and speculation data. It was aimed at the off-exchange and offshore trading many blamed for the 2008 price spike.
The NOPEC provision strips sovereign immunity and act-of-state protections, making it illegal for foreign states to jointly limit production or fix oil prices and opening them to US antitrust suits.

industries.industry: Petroleum and fuel retailers and distributors
industries.note: During declared energy emergencies, suppliers charging unconscionably excessive prices would face civil penalties of up to three times the profit and criminal penalties up to $5 million and five years in prison, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers and efficient vehicle and appliance makers
industries.note: The trust fund would finance purchases of hybrid and energy-efficient vehicles and appliances and fund renewable energy R&D grants, creating demand for these products.
